answer: Amber reached its highest value in the 4th millennium BCE (4000–3001 BCE). Based on the annual interpolated amber Z-score series (Amber_inter), the maximum value is Z = 1.54, attained as a flat-top plateau over the interval BCE 3300–3000 (CE −3300 to −3000; calBP 5250–4950, with calBP = 1950 − CE). Within that 301-row plateau, 300 annual rows fall in the 4th millennium BCE and only the single boundary year BCE 3000 (start of the 3rd millennium BCE) also reaches 1.54, so by any aggregate measure the peak millennium is the 4th millennium BCE. The finding is confirmed by the raw 100-year nodes (Amber) and by capital.csv Zamber (maximum 1.54 at BCE 3300–3000). As a robustness check, the sustained high window (Amber_inter ≥ 1.46) spans BCE 4000–2994 (calBP 5950–4944). In summary: amber peaked in the 4th millennium BCE, with its peak interval at BCE 3300–3000 (calBP 5250–4950), the flat plateau at the maximum Z = 1.54.

payload.hypothesis: Amber had its highest value (Z = 1.54) in the 4th millennium BCE, peaking in the interval BCE 3300-3000 (CE -3300 to -3000; calBP 5250-4950), the flat plateau at the maximum; a broader sustained-high window (>=1.46) spans BCE 4000-2994 (calBP 5950-4944).
